name: Thalassery (Tellicherry) biryani
tagline: Iconic Malabar biryani made with short‑grain kaima rice
summary: A fragrant Malabar biryani from Thalassery using short‑grain kaima/jeerakasala rice, light spices and a dum style that draws on coastal Mappila traditions.
description: Thalassery biryani (also called Tellicherry biryani) is the distinctive Malabar variant of biryani that originates in the coastal town of Thalassery in Kannur district. Unlike many North Indian biryanis it uses short‑grained kaima/jeerakasala rice and a lighter, aromatic spice blend rooted in local Mappila and Indian Ocean trade influences.

It matters because it represents a living local food tradition: a coastal recipe shaped by Arab and Malabar trade routes and adapted by households and restaurant kitchens across northern Kerala. The rice, layering and relatively restrained spice profile make it recognisably different from basmati biryanis.

Visitors get a bowl that balances tender meat or seafood, ghee, warm spices and the distinct texture of kaima rice; biryani in Thalassery is eaten with simple sides (raita, salna or curry) and is often the centrepiece of celebrations, festive menus and food‑tour circuits in Malabar.

For food tourists the town doubles as a culinary base: beyond the biryani you'll find related Malabar dishes, bakeries, roadside 'thattukada' snacks and coastal seafood preparations — all of which give context to the biryani experience.
highlights: Light, aromatic Malabar spice mix and ghee‑rich finish
Rooted in Mappila/coastal trade cuisine of Malabar
Available across family kitchens, famous local eateries and regional food festivals

sections.heading: Background
body: Thalassery biryani develops from Malabar’s coastal culinary history and the Mappila community’s adaptations of seasoned rice dishes. The recipe foregrounds kaima (jeerakasala) — a short, fragrant rice grain prized in Kerala — and uses a spice approach that is aromatic and restrained compared with many North Indian biryanis.

Scholars and local cooks link the biryani’s shape to centuries of trade across the Indian Ocean: spices and cooking ideas arrived via Arab traders and were absorbed into local kitchens, producing a biryani that is both regional and distinctively Kerala.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Taste it at established Thalassery restaurants and family run kitchens across town — look for places that advertise 'kaima' or 'jeerakasala' biryani. Try chicken, mutton or seafood versions; each gives a slightly different expression of the same rice and spice logic.

Combine a biryani stop with a short heritage walk (Tellicherry Fort, local markets, bakeries) and sample Malabar accompaniments like salna (thin curry), pickles and curd‑based raitas. Winter months see food festivals and special menus in Kerala and beyond where Thalassery biryani is often showcased.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Thalassery is easily reached by rail (Thalassery railway station, station code TLY), by road on NH66 and from Kannur International Airport (about 25–30 km). The best season to combine food sightseeing with comfortable weather is the cooler, drier months (roughly November–February).

If you are following a biryani circuit, book popular restaurants in advance during peak season and ask whether they use kaima rice. For local festivals or special events confirm dates with organisers before travel.

etiquette: Ask whether the restaurant uses kaima/jeerakasala rice if you want the classic texture and aroma.
Biryani is often served with salna, raita or pickles — try small portions of accompaniments to compare styles.
If you prefer milder spice, request a gentler level — local kitchens can adjust heat.
Peak season and festival weekends get busy — book ahead and confirm festival dates before travel.
